source: Kramer et al. (2023) Automated Scientific Discovery: From Equation Discovery to Autonomous Discovery Systems
finding: Review of the older line. BACON (Langley) found laws by watching pairs of variables with all else held fixed, and by building new terms (ratios, products) with production rules until one stays near constant. It re-derives Kepler's third law as D^3/P^2 = k this way.
numbers: BACON.1 to BACON.5 built on the PRISM production system. Noise handled by one tolerance parameter that decides when a term counts as constant.
limits: Needs ceteris paribus data, which the review calls a strong assumption. Later systems (Lagrange, Lagramge, SINDy, AI Feynman 2.0) handle observational data and ODEs.
agent_relevance: The BACON loop is a code-run search: build a term, test constancy within a tolerance, keep or discard. This is a counted check, not a model opinion (G5). Our agent can reuse the tolerance-based pass test as its code check.

source: Kramer et al. (2023) Automated Scientific Discovery: From Equation Discovery to Autonomous Discovery Systems (history of descendants)
finding: The review traces BACON to equation-discovery systems that use grammars (Lagramge, ProGED) and sparse regression (SINDy), then to symbolic regression. The main change over time is that the search space grows and the data conditions loosen. The basic generate-and-test loop stays.
numbers: Systems named: BACON.1-5, Lagrange, Lagramge, ProGED, SINDy, AI Feynman 2.0.
limits: Review only; it reports no head-to-head numbers in the sections read.
agent_relevance: Every modern LLM equation system (LLM-SR, SR-Scientist) is the same loop with an LLM as the proposer. So the old ablation question 'which step is essential' can be asked again with LLMs.

source: Shojaee et al. (2024/2025) LLM-SR: Scientific Equation Discovery via Programming with Large Language Models (ICLR 2025)
finding: LLM-SR has the LLM write equation skeletons as Python code, fits the constants with BFGS or Adam, scores them, and feeds the best back in context. It beat symbolic-regression baselines on four problems using about 1000 times fewer iterations.
numbers: LLM-SR ran about 2.5K iterations (4 skeletons per prompt, temperature 0.8, 2 in-context examples). Baselines (PySR, DSR, uDSR, GPlearn, NeSymReS, E2E) ran over 2M iterations. E. coli growth OOD NMSE 0.0037 for LLM-SR (GPT-3.5) versus above 1 for other methods.
limits: Backbones were GPT-3.5 and Mixtral, small by 2026 standards. Four problems only, authors' own benchmark. Table columns partly garbled in text extraction, so only the quoted E. coli figure is used.
agent_relevance: Generate skeleton, fit constants in code, score, feed back is the schema's generate-test-revise loop. The score is computed by code, so it fits G2 and G5.

source: Shojaee et al. (2024/2025) LLM-SR: Scientific Equation Discovery via Programming with Large Language Models (ICLR 2025) ablation
finding: Removing parts of LLM-SR hurt. Removing the written problem description (prior) hurt a lot. Removing the numeric refinement loop hurt a lot. Letting the LLM write full equations with constants (no skeleton plus optimizer) hurt a lot. Removing program form hurt less.
numbers: Oscillation 2, GPT-3.5. w/o iterative refinement NMSE 1.01e-1 (ID) and 1.81e-1 (OOD). w/o skeleton+optimizer NMSE 3.78e-1 (ID) and 3.75e-1 (OOD). w/o prior and w/o program: worse ('considerable' and 'less severe'; values only in a figure).
limits: One problem. Appendix: numpy+BFGS did slightly better than torch+Adam, which the authors credit to the LLM writing numpy code better.
agent_relevance: Answers 'which steps are essential' for an LLM BACON: the code-side constant fit and the feedback loop matter most. Do not let the model guess numbers; let code fit them (G2, G5).

source: Shojaee et al. (2024/2025) LLM-SR: Scientific Equation Discovery via Programming with Large Language Models (ICLR 2025) appendix: memorization of Feynman
finding: On the Feynman equations LLM-SR reached low error within fewer than 20 iterations. The authors read this as recitation of memorized formulas, not discovery. Perplexity of the Feynman equations under Mixtral was much lower than for their new problems.
numbers: Fewer than 20 iterations to low error on Feynman problems; recitation examples shown for I.37.4 and I.26.2. Perplexity values are in an appendix figure and not copied.
limits: Memorization shown by speed and perplexity, not by a direct test of training data.
agent_relevance: Key boundary condition for our own tests: a model that 'rediscovers' a famous law may be recalling it. A schema test needs problems with changed or invented laws (G3: pass must be on something the answer was not fitted to).

source: Shojaee et al. (2024/2025) LLM-SR: Scientific Equation Discovery via Programming with Large Language Models (ICLR 2025) appendix: LLM baselines
finding: Earlier LLM-based search methods (LMX, FunSearch) did worse than LLM-SR. Classic symbolic regression (DSR, uDSR, PySR) did better than those earlier LLM methods on the oscillator tasks.
numbers: Oscillator problems, Table 4 in appendix. Ablating skeleton+optimizer in LLM-SR still beat LMX and FunSearch.
limits: Only the oscillator tasks.
agent_relevance: A bare LLM-as-proposer is not enough; the structure around it (fit step, buffer) carries much of the gain. Matches G7: show the scaffold pays at equal budget.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: A New Benchmark for Scientific Equation Discovery with Large Language Models
finding: A benchmark built to resist memorization. LSR-Transform rewrites Feynman problems into less common forms (111 problems). LSR-Synth makes new synthetic problems in chemistry, biology, physics, materials (128 problems). Best system found about a third of the equations.
numbers: 239 problems total. Best symbolic accuracy 31.5% on LSR-Transform and 28.1% on LSR-Synth (as stated in the paper text). Direct prompting without data (GPT-4o-mini) 7.21% symbolic accuracy on LSR-Transform.
limits: Symbolic accuracy is judged by an LLM (GPT-4o) comparing equation forms; this adds judge noise.
agent_relevance: Gives a realistic ceiling: with memorization removed, the best LLM+search loop solves under a third. Our schema claims should be tested against this level, not against Feynman.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: A New Benchmark for Scientific Equation Discovery with Large Language Models (memorization gap)
finding: At the same expression-tree size, LSR-Transform problems were much harder than the original Feynman problems. Even small trees (0 to 15 nodes) showed the gap, so it is not just complexity. The authors say sharp drops in numeric accuracy suggest memorization.
numbers: Figure 4 compares averages over all methods and backbones; per-bin values only in the figure. LaSR on LSR-Transform: Acc0.1 45.94% to 50.45%, symbolic accuracy 5.41% to 12.61%. LLM-SR Acc0.1 38.55%, 10.81%, 39.64% (Llama-8B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4o-mini).
limits: Numeric match (Acc0.1) is high while symbolic match is low: fitting the numbers is not finding the law.
agent_relevance: Direct echo of G3: a fit is not proof. Our check should test the form on points far from the fitted data, not just error on given data.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) LLM-SRBench: A New Benchmark for Scientific Equation Discovery with Large Language Models (OOD)
finding: Symbolic accuracy and out-of-domain numeric accuracy move together. Methods that found the right form generalised; others had higher OOD error.
numbers: Strong positive correlation of symbolic accuracy with OOD Acc0.1, negative with OOD NMSE (Fig. 6, averaged over LSR-Synth domains; correlation value in figure only).
limits: Synthetic problems; correlation, not causal.
agent_relevance: An OOD point check is a cheap code-side proxy for 'right law'. Use it as the held-out test (G3).

source: Sharlin and Josephson (2024/2026) In Context Learning and Reasoning for Symbolic Regression with Large Language Models
finding: GPT-4 and GPT-4o were prompted with data, scientific context, and a scratchpad; code optimised and scored each guess and fed results back. Both rediscovered Langmuir adsorption. GPT-4o did better on dual-site Langmuir and on Nikuradse pipe flow.
numbers: Ablations on Langmuir and dual-site Langmuir: no context, no data, no scratchpad, all tools. Score = runs out of five that recovered the target at each iteration. Temperature tested at 0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1; 0.7 performed best. Per-run counts are in figures only.
limits: Five runs per setting. Dual-site Langmuir fits data almost as well as simpler forms, so it is hard to tell apart by fit alone.
agent_relevance: Scratchpad notes about data patterns (reasoning before proposing) helped. G1 says no scheduled doubt; here the scratchpad is analysis of real output, which fits G2.

source: Sharlin and Josephson (2024/2026) In Context Learning and Reasoning for Symbolic Regression with Large Language Models (leakage)
finding: Hubble's law, Kepler's law and Bode's law datasets were too leaky to use in the main text. The scientific context alone often let the model name the law and give the equation in the first iterations, and planetary period data was recognised even without context because it appears on Wikipedia.
numbers: Results for these sets moved to supplement section 5.2. No pass rates quoted in the main text.
limits: Leakage is stated by authors, not measured against training data.
agent_relevance: Kepler's third law, the classic BACON target, is now a recall test for LLMs. Do not use it as evidence that a schema step reproduces a discovery.

source: Sharlin and Josephson (2024/2026) In Context Learning and Reasoning for Symbolic Regression with Large Language Models (constraints)
finding: Adding symbolic constraints from background knowledge in the prompt made the models produce meaningful equations more often. It did not beat PySR or BMS when target equations were more complex.
numbers: Constraint-pass comparison against PySR and BMS (figure 15; PySR and BMS data taken from earlier work); no single headline number in the text read.
limits: GPT-4o only in the comparison.
agent_relevance: Constraints written as checkable rules (dimensions, positivity) can be run by code to reject candidates. Candidate for the check step.

source: Song et al. (2025) LLM-Feynman: Leveraging Large Language Models for Universal Scientific Formula and Knowledge Discovery
finding: LLM-Feynman combines LLM-guided symbolic regression, self-evaluation by the LLM, and Monte Carlo tree search. It beat AI Feynman on 100 simple and 20 complex Feynman Lectures formulas when noise was added.
numbers: 100 simple formulas: no noise both 100%; noise 1e-3: 100% vs AI Feynman 85%; noise 1e-2: 86% vs 67%. 20 complex formulas at noise 1e-2: 90% vs 55%. Abstract claims over 90% of fundamental formulas rediscovered. Used ChemLLM.
limits: Feynman formulas are famous and likely memorized (see c05, c08), so gains may partly be recall. The LLM self-evaluates with domain knowledge, which G5 warns against as a final selector.
agent_relevance: Shows LLM knowledge helps most under noise. Our check must still be code, not the model's own self-evaluation.

source: Song et al. (2025) LLM-Feynman: Leveraging Large Language Models for Universal Scientific Formula and Knowledge Discovery (ablation)
finding: On a materials task, a data-only LLM variant slightly beat the baseline, adding domain knowledge gave simpler formulas, and adding knowledge-based self-evaluation lowered error further.
numbers: Three variants compared (data-driven, plus domain knowledge, full with self-evaluation) on adsorption-energy formulas; numeric R2 values only in figure 2a-b.
limits: Single application; no reference formula for scoring there.
agent_relevance: Domain knowledge in the prompt as a simplifier (shorter formulas) is a measurable effect; fits the schema idea of using stored background as a prior.

source: Grayeli et al. (2024) Symbolic Regression with a Learned Concept Library (LaSR)
finding: LaSR runs a normal genetic search but adds LLM steps that use a growing library of plain-text concepts taken from the best equations so far. It solved more of the 100 Feynman equations than all baselines.
numbers: Exact-match solves out of 100: LaSR 72, PySR 59, uDSR 40, AI Feynman 38, AFP-FE 26, AFP 24, DSR 23, GPlearn 20. A cascade starting with llama3-8b at small LLM mixing probability already beat PySR. Ablating concept library, concept evolution, or variable names each slowed the search.
limits: Feynman set, so memorization is a concern (see c05, c08). SR-Scientist later found LaSR much weaker on a memorization-controlled set than SR-Scientist itself.
agent_relevance: Concept library = a store of lessons from past successes reused as hints. A small, code-gated version could sit in our agent's memory.

source: Xia et al. (2025/2026) SR-Scientist: Scientific Equation Discovery With Agentic AI (ICLR 2026)
finding: SR-Scientist turns the LLM into a long-horizon agent with two code tools (a data analyser and an equation evaluator) plus an experience buffer of top equations. It beat LLM-SR and LaSR by 6 to 35 points absolute on four science areas. An RL-trained version improved a small model.
numbers: Best backbone GPT-OSS-120B: Acc0.01 63.57%, Acc0.001 49.35%. Max 25 turns per iteration, about 1000 LLM calls total, three repeats averaged. 1024 problems used for RL training.
limits: Own benchmark (LSR-Synth style). Authors dropped LSR-Transform because nearly 50% of its problems reached small error after the first iteration, a sign of memorization.
agent_relevance: The most direct evidence that an agent loop with real code feedback beats a fixed proposer pipeline. Supports giving our agent tools that return real output (G2).

source: Xia et al. (2025/2026) SR-Scientist: Scientific Equation Discovery With Agentic AI (ICLR 2026) ablation
finding: Removing the data-analysis tool hurt most for GPT-OSS-120B; removing the experience buffer or top-k feedback hurt the Qwen and GLM backbones most.
numbers: Acc0.01 / Acc0.001. GPT-OSS-120B full 63.57/49.35; w/o data analyser 35.66/16.28; w/o experience 57.36/41.86; w/o top-k 58.14/41.86. Qwen3-Coder-480B full 49.09/24.55; w/o analyser 41.08/14.73; w/o experience 35.66/16.28; w/o top-k 26.36/13.70. GLM-4.5-Air full 48.32/25.06; w/o analyser 46.51/22.48; w/o experience 37.21/18.61; w/o top-k 41.96/21.71.
limits: Which component matters depends on the backbone; no single essential step across all three. Table labels read from text extraction.
agent_relevance: Gives the ablation answer for the subfield question: look at real data via code, and remember best past attempts. Both are in line with our schema; the weight differs by model, so test per model.

source: Xia et al. (2025/2026) SR-Scientist: Scientific Equation Discovery With Agentic AI (ICLR 2026) noise and classic baselines
finding: Classic symbolic regression without LLMs scored near zero on this memorization-controlled set. LLM methods scored far higher. Accuracy of all methods fell as noise rose, with SR-Scientist staying above the others.
numbers: Without-LLM rows (DSR, uDSR, PySR, GPLearn, E2E, NeSymReS) show 0.00 to about 3% Acc0.01 overall in Table 1.
limits: Row labels partly garbled in text extraction. Noise results in Fig. 3 only; no number copied.
agent_relevance: On new problems the LLM prior is what helps, not just search. But the prior can also be recall, so keep a changed-law control.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) NewtonBench: Benchmarking Generalizable Scientific Law Discovery in LLM Agents (ICLR 2026)
finding: 324 law-discovery tasks in 12 physics domains: 108 counterfactual shifted laws in three settings (plain equation, simple system, complex system). Agents run experiments on a simulated system. Frontier reasoning models can find shifted laws in simple systems, but fall off sharply in complex ones.
numbers: 11 LLMs. Non-thinking models (GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3) under 10% symbolic accuracy overall. GPT-5 75.9% and Gemini-2.5-pro 65.4% overall. Hardest setting: GPT-5 40.3%, Gemini-2.5-pro 16.7%, all other reasoning models under 6%.
limits: Simulated physics with a formula checker; shifted laws still resemble known ones.
agent_relevance: Changed-law design is the right control for rediscovery tests. Reasoning models do far better than plain ones, so scaffold gains must be measured on the reasoning-model baseline.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) NewtonBench: Benchmarking Generalizable Scientific Law Discovery in LLM Agents (ICLR 2026) noise and code
finding: Accuracy is very fragile to noise. A code interpreter helped weak models and slightly hurt strong ones, because strong models stopped exploring and took the first good-enough fit.
numbers: Noise of just 0.0001 cut accuracy 12 to 16% relative to noise-free; accuracy fell steadily to 0.1. Code helped models with symbolic accuracy under 40%, hurt those at 40% or more. Gemini-2.5-flash exploration rate fell sharply when code budget went from zero to one; Qwen-3-235b stayed steady.
limits: Exploration rate comes from two models with visible reasoning traces only.
agent_relevance: Strong warning: giving code tools can trigger early satisficing. This argues for a held-out check before stopping, and for a forced alternatives step only on a failure signal (G1).

source: Yang et al. (2026) Think like a Scientist: Physics-guided LLM Agent for Equation Discovery (KeplerAgent)
finding: KeplerAgent first uses physics tools to find structure (such as symmetries), then uses that to configure PySINDy and PySR. This copies how a scientist narrows the hypothesis space before fitting.
numbers: Algebraic benchmark: with 3 parallel attempts symbolic accuracy 42.34%, above PySR and LLM-SR at similar runtime and tokens. Single attempt beats LLM-SR, but default PySR (many iterations, many operators) beats the single attempt, at much longer runtime.
limits: Own benchmarks; authors' tools; best number is with 3 attempts.
agent_relevance: Structure first, then search: a staged order of operators. Matches our idea of S-states with code-run steps, and supports 'narrow before fit'.

source: Yang et al. (2026) Think like a Scientist: Physics-guided LLM Agent for Equation Discovery (KeplerAgent) differential equations
finding: On 10 coupled-equation systems (20 equations), KeplerAgent was much better than baselines on noisy data.
numbers: Noisy data: 45% symbolic accuracy, about 3 times the best baseline, and order-of-magnitude lower NMSE (pointwise and long-term).
limits: Small benchmark (10 systems). A case study in the appendix shows the agent stuck at 15.6% MAPE on noisy data and not learning from its earlier attempts.
agent_relevance: The appendix failure (not learning from earlier tries) is a gap our experience store should fill.

source: Jansen et al. (2024) DiscoveryWorld: A Virtual Environment for Developing and Evaluating Automated Scientific Discovery Agents
finding: Text world with 120 tasks (8 topics, 3 difficulty levels). Agents must form hypotheses, run experiments and explain. Baseline LLM agents did poorly; humans did far better.
numbers: Human scientists (16 tasks): 66% completion, 55% explanatory knowledge. Best agent ReAct: 38% of easy tasks and 18% of challenge tasks. Best at knowledge (Hypothesizer): 34% of gold knowledge on easy, 8% on challenge. Unit-test sub-skills about 60%+.
limits: Models are 2024-era (GPT-4 class); cost estimate USD 3k to 10k for a full run.
agent_relevance: Fully invented worlds remove memorization, so this is a clean test. Agents are fine at parts (measuring) but not the whole loop: the planner state machine is what is missing.

source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench: Towards Data-Driven Discovery with Large Language Models
finding: Benchmark of data-driven hypothesis discovery from real and synthetic datasets, scored by hypothesis match. Best framework got 25%. Domain knowledge hints raised the score.
numbers: Best non-oracle agent peaks at 25% hypothesis match. DataVoyager (GPT-4) archaeology tasks: 9.9% vs 17.5% with added domain knowledge (the paper text words the two arms in the reverse order, but the sense is that hints helped). Biology 0%, engineering 7%, economics 25%, sociology 23%. Oracle-reflection variant retries up to 3 times using the true match score.
limits: Oracle score use is a ceiling, not a deployable setting. Replicating datasets for the benchmark took up to 90 person-hours each.
agent_relevance: Domain facts as extra context matter. The oracle-reflect loop shows how large gains from a perfect check could be; real checks are weaker (G3).

source: Wang et al. (2026) FIRE-Bench: Evaluating AI Agents on the Rediscovery of Scientific Insights
finding: Agents get only a research question from a recent ML paper and must run experiments and reach the paper's finding. Even the best coding agents scored under 50 F1, with large run-to-run swings.
numbers: 30 core tasks plus 10 cross-domain; 100 papers in release. F1: Claude Code (Sonnet-4) 46.7 (sd 23.4), Codex (gpt-5-medium) 41.9, OpenHands gpt-5 37.9, OpenHands o4-mini 31.9. Median coefficient of variation across tasks 0.37 for Claude Code, over 0.6 for OpenHands. Judge validated at precision 0.95, recall 0.86, F1 0.89.
limits: Rediscovery of ML empirical findings, not natural laws. Claude Code omitted from some extensions for cost.
agent_relevance: Variance across runs is large; one run proves little. Use repeated runs when comparing schema versus plain.

source: Wang et al. (2026) FIRE-Bench: Evaluating AI Agents on the Rediscovery of Scientific Insights failure analysis
finding: Most errors were in research planning (method or goal deviation) and in forming conclusions (unsupported or overgeneralised claims), not coding. Wrong claims were mostly contradictory or unrelated, rarely valid alternatives.
numbers: Contradictory plus unrelated made 76.4% to 95.0% of false-positive claims by agent; alternative conclusions only 4.5% to 10.9%. Swapping OpenHands backbone o4-mini to gpt-5 raised F1 from 31.9 to 37.9 (+6.1). Weakest part: designing controls.
limits: Error labels made by LLM plus author review.
agent_relevance: The loss is at design of controls and at conclusion from evidence, which are the schema's check states. Worth targeting with code-run checks that compare claim to actual output (G2).

source: Wang et al. (2026) FIRE-Bench: Evaluating AI Agents on the Rediscovery of Scientific Insights contamination check
finding: Tasks published after a model's cutoff were not harder to solve than before it, once difficulty is held fixed. So no strong sign that memory of the paper drives scores.
numbers: Hard tasks, pre to post cutoff F1: o4-mini 15.4 to 24.8; gpt-5 22.6 to 31.0. Medium: o4-mini 31.9 to 33.6; gpt-5 44.5 to 23.1. Easy: o4-mini 58.9 to 42.1.
limits: Authors say the test is coarse: cutoff dates approximate, small groups.
agent_relevance: A usable way to check recall risk: compare tasks before and after the cutoff within difficulty bands.

source: Yang et al. (2025) MOOSE-Chem: Large Language Models for Rediscovering Unseen Chemistry Scientific Hypotheses (ICLR 2025)
finding: Hypotheses are split into three steps: retrieve inspirations from the literature, compose a hypothesis from background plus inspiration, rank hypotheses. A staged agent rediscovered many held-out hypotheses from 51 papers published after January 2024.
numbers: Inspiration retrieval, GPT-4o: Hit Ratio 96.7% when the top 20% of a 300-paper corpus is kept, 83.7% at top 4%, 60.8% at top 0.8%. Llama-3.1-8B at top 4%: 43.5%; 70B: 83.0%. Matched score (0-5, GPT-4o judge) Top MS 4.020 vs MOOSE 2.882, SciMON 2.549. w/o multi-step 3.765; w/o multi-step and ranking 2.863.
limits: Match scored by GPT-4o (Claude and Gemini judges in appendix). Chemistry, small benchmark. Models trained before the papers appeared limit contamination.
agent_relevance: A decomposition into retrieve, compose, rank, with screening in staged rounds. Fits our S-states. The judge is an LLM, which G5 treats with care.

source: Cornelio et al. (2025) The Need for Verification in AI-Driven Scientific Discovery
finding: Review that argues that checking candidates against data and theory is what gives discovery its value. Appendix tests GPT-5 on the AI Descartes binary-star data, which encodes Kepler's third law, with variables renamed to hide the problem.
numbers: GPT-5 tried several forms (a small symbolic regression) and did not produce the target form period = d^3/(m1+m2). On a separate simple derivation-from-axioms task, GPT-4 failed and GPT-5 gave the right formula and derivation.
limits: Two anecdotal prompts, not a benchmark. The review says LLM methods have less controllable inductive biases and are sensitive to prompt wording.
agent_relevance: With names hidden, a frontier model did not recall Kepler's law from the data alone. Renaming variables is a cheap recall control we can copy.

source: Fang et al. (2025) AI-Newton: A Concept-Driven Physical Law Discovery System without Prior Physical Knowledge
finding: A system (not shown in the text read to use an LLM at its core) that proposes concepts such as mass and force, builds laws, and generalises them across experiments without physics prior. It rediscovered Newton's second law, energy conservation, and universal gravitation from simulated noisy mechanics data.
numbers: Max 1200 trials, average runtime 48 hours, about 90 concepts and 50 general laws per test case on average, 10 test cases. It finds simple concepts (mass) before complex ones (force).
limits: Data are simulated; the building blocks are human-designed; long run time.
agent_relevance: Closest modern version of BACON's staged build-up of terms. Shows order matters: simple concepts first, then use them to define harder ones.
